subject: Analogies to Stan's handling of missing data

messages.author: b70e5a419fc15914
messages.subject: Analogies to Stan's handling of missing data
parts:
Hi All,

First off, thanks very much to the developers of Stan.  I've been using it in a great deal.  It solves a number of problems that I would have if I were to use other programs, all in one go.  I'm also really excited to see new features being added (parallelization, WAIC and loo, etc.).  

I've got a data set with some missing data.  I've read previous threads on this topic, and the documentation in the User's Guide, which have explained how to write the model.  I'm trying to figure out how to write this up for a manuscript, in a way that someone unfamiliar with Stan would understand.  My sense is that Stan is using the parameter estimates for observed data to inform the estimates for missing data in a way that is similar to a specially-made imputation algorithm (in which the imputation model is exactly the same as the analysis model).  Is this accurate?  If so, would the estimates from Stan asymptotically approach estimates from FIML, just as infinite imputations would?

Thanks for your thoughts.  

Best wishes,
Katherine

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Analogies to Stans' handling of missing data
parts:
Stan's handling of missing data, like that of JAGS and BUGS,
is the standard Bayesian approach, where the missing data are just
treated like other parameters. So you're defining a joint
density p(y, y_miss, theta) where y is observed data, y_miss
is missing data, and theta are the usual parameters. Then
you get inference for the posterior p(y_miss, theta | y) in
the usual way. Nothing special about "missing data" per se.

So it's not like a standalone imputation system (multiple or
otherwise), where you do the imputation, then plug the imputed
values into the "full data" model. Rather all the inference is
joint.

I don't know what FIML is or what you mean by infinite imputations.

Asymptotpics are tricky here as you have to carefully design what's
growing; usually the data related to imputing the missing data doesn't
grow, as in when you have missing predictors for an item and you impute
them based on the other predictors (and perhaps the outcome).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Analogies to Stans' handling of missing data
parts:
Thanks for the explanation.  FIML is full-information maximum likelihood:

Enders, C. K., & Bandalos, D. L. (2001). The relative performance of full information maximum likelihood estimation for missing data in structural equation models. Structural Equation Modeling, 8(3), 430-457.

The readers of the journal I'm submitting to are familiar with FIML, and might have heard of multiple imputation, but Bayesian statistics are a little outside of the norm.  I would like to provide a compelling argument for why Stan's handling of missing data is appropriate.  I know the posteriors will also depend to some extent on the prior, which would complicate a direct comparison of missing data in Bayesian and ML estimation, but a reference showing that Bayesian methods are unbiased would be helpful.  When I search for articles, most of the results concern Bayesian methods for imputing missing data p(y_miss | y), rather than the accuracy and precision of the estimate of the joint density p(y, y_miss, theta).

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Analogies to Stans' handling of missing data
parts:
Hi, we can do maximum likelihood in Stan, but typical uses of Stan will be for Bayesian inference.  When we do maximum likelihood, it’s usually because it might be a useful computational approximation.

Bayesian methods will not be unbiased in the formal statistical sense.  We discuss this in our BDA book:  look up “unbiased” in the index and you can see our discussion.  The short answer is that classical unbiasedness is not generally a good thing!
A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Analogies to Stans' handling of missing data
parts:
Rather than bias, we worry about calibration. That is,
if we give a 50% or 95% interval for a parameter, is there
a 50% or 95% chance it's in that interval?

With hierarchical models, you do partial pooling, which
introduces a bit of classical "bias" (toward the population mean),
which in turn reduces variance enough that the predictions are much
sharper (narrower 95% intervals for where a parameter's value is),
while remaining well calibrated.

The next level up we need to fix priors, but these can be weakly
informative and typically aren't very sensitive (change in posterior given
change in prior) in the sense that reasonable changes in the prior do
not produce noticeable changes in the posterior.

- Bob

messages.author: b70e5a419fc15914
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Analogies to Stans' handling of missing data
parts:
Great.  Thank you very much Andrew and Ben.

Has anyone performed simulation studies comparing parameter calibration when missing data are listwise deleted versus treated as unknown parameters, across various types of missingness (missing at random, missing completely at random, missing not at random)?  These explanations make logical sense, but it would be nice to have a citation demonstrating how these principles play out.

For what it's worth, the parameters in my model don't appear to have changed much between a version fit to complete cases only (80% of the total N) and a version incorporating partially missing cases.

Katherine

There are whole books on missing data imputation
of various kinds. I don't understand the contrast
between listwise deleted vs. treated as unknown parameters.

There's also a huge semi-supervised learning literature
in machine learning, where the outcome y is missing. There
can be big differences there, especially in data with long
tails like that in natural language.

- Bob

My sense is that Stan is using the parameter estimates for observed data to inform the estimates for missing data in a way that is similar to a specially-made imputation algorithm (in which the imputation model is exactly the same as the analysis model). Is this accurate? If so, would the estimates from Stan asymptotically approach estimates from FIML, just as infinite imputations would?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Analogies to Stans' handling of missing data
parts:
On Wednesday, March 30, 2016 at 8:09:20 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I don't understand the contrast
between listwise deleted vs. treated as unknown parameters.

List-wise deletion is just dropping any observations with a missing value on at least one of the variables in the model. So in a regression context, dropping any row of X with at least one missing value. It's pretty much always a bad idea. And even if it can be justified under an MCAR assumption (very rare) you can lose a lot of data. 

Jonah

messages.author: 83aa4ea66d984b54
messages.subject: Re: Analogies to Stan's handling of missing data
parts: Katherine, if you're doing structural equation models (as your FIML reference suggests) then stick to your guns on Stan, including the joint Bayesian estimation of the missing data. You probably know the Song & Lee book on Bayesian SEMs (if not, I *highly* recommend it), and that gives a number of very strong arguments for Bayes in preference to any of the other wacky (as they seem to me) ways of estimating SEMs.
